scenes.name: El soul conquista Gran Bretaña
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 26 de octubre «Reach Out I’ll Be There» de los Four Tops, con la flauta de aire oriental, el fraseo dylaniano de Lamont Dozier y la interpretación de su vida de Levi Stubbs, desbancó a «Distant Drums» y fue número 1: el momento en que la música negra americana ocupó el centro de la cultura juvenil británica, al revés que en el boom del beat. Lo habían preparado durante años los entusiastas: Dave Godin, que fundó en 1963 la Tamla Motown Appreciation Society, viajó a Detroit, llevó «Where Did Our Love Go» a los piratas y bautizó el sello Tamla Motown (marzo de 1965, con una gira de la revista que fracasó fuera de Londres); Guy Stevens, que pinchaba discos negros en el Scene y dirigió Sue Records para Chris Blackwell; Roger Eagle en el Twisted Wheel de Mánchester; Tony Hall promocionando Atlantic («In the Midnight Hour», el «My Girl» de Otis Redding); el DJ Jeff Dexter mezclando soul y ska en Tiles, el club subterráneo de Oxford Street del mod de masas que visitó Tom Wolfe. En otoño de 1966 Atlantic y Motown copaban las listas; Otis Redding metió a 8.000 personas en Tiles; los Four Tops arrasaron en el Savile de Brian Epstein el 13 de noviembre. El racismo, aun así, seguía ahí.

scenes.name: Ska y rocksteady en Londres
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Savage dejó fuera el ska por la casi imposibilidad de fechar los discos, pero estaba en todas partes: Peter Meaden veía en 1964 un movimiento mod que solo tenía pop americano, R&B y «una pizca de ska jamaicano»; Island editó desde 1963 una avalancha de ska y Chris Blackwell diversificó con Sue; en Le Duce y en Tiles sonaban Prince Buster, Desmond Dekker o los Wailers, y en Tiles el ska llegó a dominar: «cualquiera podía bailar un disco de ska», y por primera vez la juventud negra se mezclaba en los clubes. La discografía del libro recoge algunos sencillos del año.

podcast.title: Nearly Quit Music for James Bond (1962)
podcast.body: In 1962, Blackwell nearly abandoned his music career. Thanks to family connections, he got a job as a go-fer and had a cameo role in the first James Bond film, "Dr. No." Producer Harry Saltzman offered him a permanent job, but a fortune teller advised Blackwell to stick with music. "He'd been given a job as a go-for on the first James Bond film, Dr No, thanks to his family connections, and had also had a cameo role in the film."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Bringing Millie Small to UK (1963)
podcast.body: In 1963, Blackwell identified Millie Small's potential for international stardom. He convinced her mother to allow Millie to move to the UK, promising to make her a star, and subsequently licensed her records to Fontana for wider distribution. "in 1963 he had decided to call Milly's mother and promise her that if a daughter came over to the UK, he would be able to make her into a star."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Witness to Jamaican Shooting (1996)
podcast.body: Chris Blackwell, the head of Island Records, was among the friends with Bono and his family on Jimmy Buffett's plane, the "Hemisphere Dancer," when it was mistakenly fired upon by Jamaican police at Negril airport on January 16, 1996. "On January 16th 1996, Bono and his family and some friends including Jimmy Buffett and Island Records head Chris Blackwell visited Blackwell State in Jamaica."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Licensing Millie Small's Records
podcast.body: Instead of releasing Millie Small's records directly on Island, which lacked wide distribution at the time, Blackwell opted to license them to Fontana, a mid-sized British label, to ensure broader reach and impact for her first British singles. "Rather than release her records on Ireland, which didn't have any wide distribution, he decided to license them to Fontana, amidst size British label."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Mother's Social Connections & Influence
podcast.body: His mother, Blanche Blackwell, was a socialite in Jamaica known for her affairs, including with Errol Flynn and Ian Fleming. Fleming reportedly based characters like Pussy Galore and Honeychild Ryder on her. Her life and connections provided Chris with a unique perspective and entry points into Jamaican culture. "His mother, Blanche, lived in Jamaica, where she was amused to many men."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Move to England and Island Records Distribution
podcast.body: After his experience with "Dr. No" and the fortune teller's advice, Blackwell moved back to England. There, he continued to run Island Records, primarily as a distributor of Jamaican records, hand-selling them to shops in immigrant communities across London, Manchester, and Birmingham. "he moved back to England, where he continued running Island Records, this time as a distributor of Jamaican Records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Privileged Background
podcast.body: Chris Blackwell came from a privileged background; his father was an heir to the Crosse & Blackwell fortune, and he was educated at Harrow. Despite this, he spent much of his youth in Jamaica, where his mother lived. "His father had been one of the heirs to the cross-and-blackwell fortune, and young Chris had been educated at Harrow."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Producer of Millie Small's Hit
podcast.body: Chris Blackwell, an Englishman, produced Millie Small's worldwide hit "My Boy Lollipop." This song was a significant milestone in bringing Jamaican Ska (SCOP/Blue Beat) music to a broader audience in Britain and internationally, facilitated by his newly established Island Records label. "The big breakthrough was a worldwide hit by Millie Small, called My Boy Lollipop, produced by Englishman Chris Blackwell, and distributed through his brand new Idle and Records label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rastafari Culture Fascination
podcast.body: Blackwell developed a deep fascination with Rastafari culture after being rescued by Rasta fishermen when his boat crashed while sailing. This experience solidified his goal to promote Jamaican culture globally. "Chris Blackwell had developed a fascination with Raster culture after having crashed his boat while sailing and being rescued by some Raster fishermen, and he had decided that his girl was to promote Jamaican culture to the world."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

xref.title: Desmond Dekker – Jamaica's Top Singer of the 1960s; Ska's First Worldwide Hit (1969); Worked in Welding Shop with Bob Marley
xref.body: Desmond Dekker used to work in a Jamaican welding shop alongside a kid from St. Anne's parish named Bob Marley. Dekker became Jamaica's top singer of the 1960s and, thanks to Island Records (run by Englishman Chris Blackwell, who was in love with Caribbean music), scored ska's first worldwide hit in 1969. "He used to work in a Jamaican welding shop along a kid from St. Anne's parish named Bob Marley."

xref.title: Death in Miami (May 1981)
xref.body: On May 8, 1981, Bob Marley decided to return home to Jamaica and asked Chris Blackwell, head of Island Records, to fly him there. However, his vital signs worsened during the flight, forcing the plane to land in Miami, where he was taken to Cedars of Lebanon Hospital. Critically ill and in immense pain, he died on May 11, 1981, surrounded by his family and weighing only 82 pounds, at the age of 36. "He was critically ill and in a tremendous amount of pain. But there was nothing the doctors could do except offer large amounts of powerful pain killers. And then, surrounded by his family and weighing just 82 pounds, Bob Marley died. It was May 11, 1981."
